title: IRS Identifies Certain CRAT Transactions as Listed Transactions: What Taxpayers and Advisors Need to Know
summary: IRS final regulations identify certain CRAT-SPIA arrangements as listed transactions, increasing disclosure obligations and compliance risks.
body_text: The IRS issued final regulations on July 9, 2026, identifying certain charitable remainder annuity trust (CRAT) arrangements as “listed transactions.” The rules focus on transactions involving a single CRAT and a single premium immediate annuity (SPIA) where taxpayers attempt to report CRAT distributions under annuity tax rules rather than under the special ordering rules that apply to CRATs. For taxpayers and advisors, these regulations signal increased IRS scrutiny of such transactions, with a “listed transaction” being a type of reportable transaction that the IRS has identified as having potential for tax avoidance and that carries heightened disclosure obligations. As with any listed transaction, Material Advisors and certain participants may be subject to reporting with respect to these transactions, as well, along with significant penalties for failing to properly disclose their involvement. Understanding CRATs and Their Traditional Use Under Section 664(c) A CRAT is an irrevocable trust that can help donors balance charitable goals with income, estate, and tax planning objectives. One of the primary tax benefits of a CRAT is that the donor may receive an upfront charitable donation income tax deduction when the CRAT is funded. The deduction is based on the present value of the charitable remainder interest that is expected to pass to charity at the end of the trust term. When properly structured, a CRAT generally is not subject to income tax at the trust level under IRC Section 664(c). The sale of appreciated assets by the trust can create a tax deferral opportunity rather than an immediate tax liability at the trust level. The deferral does not eliminate tax for the noncharitable beneficiaries. Distributions from the CRAT remain taxable to the beneficiaries under the Section 664(b) ordering rules, which require the trust’s ordinary income and capital gain to be subject to tax before any amount is treated as a return of corpus. The Transaction Drawing IRS Scrutiny (Section 72) – CRAT-SPIA Structure The transactions drawing IRS attention generally involve certain arrangements structured as CRATs funded with appreciated property. The trust uses some or all of the sale proceeds to purchase a SPIA. The beneficiary then attempts to treat the CRAT annuity payment as if it were an annuity payment governed by Section 72, rather than a trust distribution governed by the ordering rules. Section 72 can allow a portion of certain annuity payments to be treated as a recovery of investment in the annuity contract. In the CRAT-SPIA structure, taxpayers may argue that a significant portion of the beneficiary’s payment is excluded from income as a return of the SPIA investment. Treasury and the IRS view this position as a misapplication of the rules because CRAT distributions are separately governed by Section 664(b), which carries out ordinary income and capital gain to noncharitable beneficiaries before amounts are treated as corpus. Listed Transactions and Disclosure Requirements The final regulations identify certain CRAT-SPIA arrangements and substantially similar transactions, as listed transactions. This does not mean that every CRAT or every CRAT involving an annuity product is abusive. Rather, the listed transaction focuses on arrangements with specific features, including a CRAT-SPIA structure in which the beneficiary reports the CRAT annuity payment under Section 72 instead of under the Section 664(b) ordering rules. Treasury and the IRS have made clear that they view this strategy as having the potential to avoid or significantly reduce taxable gain. Under the final regulations, taxpayers who participate in an identified CRAT-SPIA transaction or a substantially similar arrangement may be required to disclose their participation to the IRS under the reportable transaction rules. Material advisors may also be subject to disclosure requirements and recordkeeping obligations. In addition, participants and material advisors may be required to provide detailed information regarding their involvement in these listed transactions. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements can result in significant penalties under the reportable transaction rules, including penalties applicable to listed transactions. Penalties for failure to disclose can reach up to $100,000 for an individual, and there is no general good-faith exception for failing to disclose a listed transaction. Charitable Remainder Organizations The final regulations provide relief for certain charitable organizations whose only role or interest in the transaction is as the charitable remainderman. The organization generally is not treated as a participant in the listed transaction and is not treated as a party to a prohibited tax shelter transaction solely because it holds the charitable remainder interest. Implications for Estate Planning and Tax Professionals Charitable planning strategies should be evaluated carefully when they promise significant tax benefits that appear inconsistent with the underlying policy of the tax rules. Estate planning and tax professionals advising on CRAT planning should review existing and proposed structures involving annuity products. The review should determine whether the arrangement falls within the identified transaction, or is substantially similar to it, and whether distributions are being reported under the Section 664 CRAT ordering rules rather than under Section 72. Advisors should evaluate potential disclosure obligations for both taxpayers and material advisors and also maintain documentation supporting the economic and charitable objectives of any legitimate CRAT arrangement. Strategic Considerations Traditional CRATs remain valuable charitable and estate planning tools when structured and administered in compliance with applicable tax rules. As the IRS continues to scrutinize sophisticated trust and charitable planning strategies, taxpayers and advisors should carefully review both new planning opportunities and existing CRAT structures, particularly those involving annuity products. Recent regulations targeting certain abusive CRAT transactions are a reminder that charitable remainder annuity trusts should be structured and administered in accordance with the applicable tax rules and their intended charitable purpose. Careful planning and ongoing oversight are essential to preserving the intended tax benefits and charitable objectives. Key Takeaways Properly structured and implemented CRATs remain valid charitable planning vehicles. Treasury and IRS have identified certain CRAT-SPIA arrangements and substantially similar transactions as listed transactions effective July 9, 2026. The targeted transactions generally involve an attempt to apply the Section 72 annuity rules rather than the Section 664(b) CRAT ordering rules to CRAT distributions. Participants and material advisors may have disclosure obligations and face penalties for noncompliance. Tax professionals should review existing and proposed CRAT arrangements involving annuity products to determine whether additional reporting may be needed. Please contact our tax professionals with any questions. Internal Revenue Service, Charitable Remainder Annuity Trust Listed Transaction , T.D. 10051, 91 Fed. Reg. 42353 (July 9, 2026). FAQ A CRAT-SPIA transaction generally involves a charitable remainder annuity trust (CRAT) that uses proceeds from the sale of appreciated assets to purchase a single premium immediate annuity (SPIA). The IRS believes some taxpayers have improperly reported CRAT distributions under Section 72 annuity rules instead of the Section 664(b) ordering rules that apply to CRATs, potentially reducing taxable income. No. The regulations target specific CRAT-SPIA arrangements and substantially similar transactions, not properly structured CRATs used for legitimate charitable and estate planning purposes. Taxpayers who participate in identified transactions and material advisors involved with them may have disclosure and recordkeeping obligations under the reportable transaction rules. Failure to comply with disclosure requirements can result in significant penalties, including penalties that may reach up to $100,000 for individuals. Review existing and proposed CRAT arrangements involving annuity products, confirm distributions are reported under the appropriate CRAT rules, and assess any potential disclosure obligations. © Copyright CBIZ, Inc. body_text: 14 Feb 2025 Artificial Intelligence For the first time in Spain, BBVA will offer AI-powered account and card management with its virtual assistant BBVA has updated its personal virtual assistant Blue, integrated in its app, making it more personalized. Blue now has enhanced abilities to interact with customers using natural language, provide tailored information on their finances, and perform some of the most common account and card transactions. In parallel, BBVA created a co-pilot to facilitate the daily work of branch employees. With these initiatives, BBVA is moving forward with its strategy to put artificial intelligence (AI) at the disposal of its customers, and mark the beginning of a new stage in digital banking management. The roll-out of the new assistant Blue, with the AI Factory team participating in the technical aspects, will take place on February 20th in Spain and gradually reach all of the bank’s customers.

title: Custom Advertising Algorithms: Definition and Real World Impact
summary: Learn how custom advertising algorithms work, why they matter in digital marketing, their benefits, challenges, and real-world examples.
body_text: Digital advertising, and specifically programmatic advertising, uses algorithms to deliver optimization and personalization in its campaigns. Custom advertising algorithms, in particular, are a series of steps programmed to adapt the targeting to specific business objectives and audiences . These algorithms, used to determine which ads are shown to which users in real time, continuously refine themselves thanks to AI and machine learning. In this article, we explore what custom advertising algorithms are, how they work, and why they matter for the future of digital advertising. Key Highlights Custom advertising algorithms adapt campaigns to specific business goals, unlike generic models. They rely on first-party data, AI, and machine learning to refine targeting and optimize in real time. Retailers, e-commerce brands, travel, finance, and healthcare see the strongest impact from tailored models. Measuring success requires looking at ROAS, CPA, and CLV, not just clicks or impressions. Building these algorithms demands time, expertise, and large datasets, but results can transform campaign performance. How do Custom Advertising Algorithms Work? A mix of data, automation, and adaptability is driving custom advertising algorithms to quickly become the standard for performance-driven campaigns. Unlike generic models, custom advertising algorithms are built with a single campaign’s objectives in mind . They use carefully selected sources and assets, ranging from brand-owned customer data to seasonal shopping trends, to align campaigns with the advertiser’s business goals. For instance, a retail store promoting winter gear doesn’t need the same algorithm as a beverages brand launching a summer cocktail. The algorithm “thinks” based on the campaign’s criteria and objectives, tailoring the logic. The digital advertising market continues to grow, and it is projected to account for over 80% of the advertising market by 2030. The demand for this level of customization is also growing. The reason? Where shelf tools may miss nuances, custom models can capture context, intent, and timing with far greater precision . Custom algorithms sift through massive streams of online data, search queries, browsing behavior, demographic details, purchase history, and even content engagement, to uncover the patterns that really matter. From there, they adjust bidding strategies, creative delivery, and audience targeting in real time. How Machine Learning and AI Drive Automation in Advertising Algorithms. Algorithms are the base of automation in programmatic advertising, and machine learning and AI make this automation possible. These technologies continuously refine the model’s rules by learning from live campaign results . For instance, which ad placements led to conversions, which audiences responded best to, and which times or platforms delivered the best returns. Over time, the algorithm’s continuous learning reduces wasted impressions. Advertisers use this information to reallocate the budget towards the most productive placement and times. This process requires processing massive amounts of data, which is handled by AI and ML algorithms. This mix of data, automation, and adaptability is why custom advertising algorithms are quickly becoming the standard for performance-driven campaigns. Outmax, Perion’s AI execution agent, runs on this exact principle: it continuously reallocates spend and pacing in real time toward whatever is performing best across YouTube, Meta, TikTok, CTV, display, and video. Custom Ad Algorithms Model Types Custom algorithms can be categorized into different models, according to their performance objective: Predictive models analyze historical and real-time data to forecast future user actions such as clicks, purchases, or churn. Using these algorithms helps advertisers anticipate trends and allocate budgets toward audiences most likely to convert. Classification models group users based on behavior, demographics, or intent, enabling precise audience segmentation and message personalization. These models reduce wasted impressions by ensuring ads reach the most relevant viewers. Recommendation models use machine learning to match users with creatives, products, or offers they’re most likely to engage with, improving click-through and conversion rates. These algorithms are especially useful in dynamic environments like retail or video advertising. Bidding optimization models automatically adjust bids in real time based on user value, competition, and campaign goals. This ensures efficient use of the budget while maximizing ROI across channels. Outmax applies this model at scale, allocating spend and pacing across each channel based on live performance signals rather than a fixed budget split. Not all algorithms conform to a single type. Multi-objective models balance trade-offs, such as reach versus cost or engagement versus conversions, by simultaneously optimizing multiple KPIs. How do Algorithms Improve Digital Advertising? Algorithms make digital advertising more accurate and easier to manage . They identify which user profile is most likely to respond to the ad and adjust the campaign accordingly. As such, if performance starts to dip, a custom algorithm can tweak bids, targeting, or ad delivery, allowing for flexible campaign adjustments. Custom algorithms provide better optimization by learning from audience behavior. Then the algorithm keeps refining the campaign to help the ad achieve the set goal. Moreover, the optimization is based on hard data . These algorithms benefit businesses with seasonal demand, especially since they can automatically scale campaigns up or down as needed. How to Measure the Success of Custom Advertising Algorithms? A custom algorithm is working if it improves campaign performance. Success starts with clear goals. Are you customizing the algorithm to cut acquisition costs, boost conversions, or stretch your advertising budget further? With those goals set, you can look at clicks and impressions to see whether the algorithm is making a dent in the campaign’s performance. Still, numbers like clicks and impressions only tell part of the story. What really matters is measuring the impact, whether the clicks are turning into customers or if the revenue is growing. Look at metrics such as return on ad spend (ROAS) , cost per acquisition (CPA) , and customer lifetime value (CLV). By doing this, you can check if the algorithm is delivering real results. You can measure impact through A/B testing. For instance, an online retailer can run two parallel campaigns, one with a custom algorithm and another with a standard boxed solution. If, when measuring impact, the algorithm has cut CPA by 20%, that’s evidence of success. Here are a few tips to measure accurately: First, monitor performance over a few weeks, not days. An extended period can give you more accurate results. Next, monitor both costs (efficiency) and sales or leads (outcomes). Third, benchmarks should be reviewed regularly to account for market changes. Challenges of Advertising Algorithms Customization Despite their benefits, building custom algorithms presents challenges. One of the biggest hurdles is the time and resources needed for development. Building an algorithm from scratch often involves weeks of data preparation, coding, and testing before it’s ready to be applied to live campaigns. Another challenge is the massive amount of data required to train the algorithm. Algorithms need large, high-quality datasets to recognize patterns and make reliable predictions. For smaller advertisers, gathering enough meaningful data can be a major challenge. There’s also the issue of transparency in the industry. title: How Autotorino automated lead intake and inbound call capture with Zapier and Salesforce
summary: How Autotorino used Zapier and AI to automate lead intake across 109 Zaps and capture 1,500+ inbound call requests a month that used to go unanswered.
body_text: Autotorino manages sales and after-sales across 74 locations and 23 brands, with customer requests arriving through web forms, lead-gen tools, email, and a high volume of phone calls. The challenge was routing: getting every interaction into the right system, in the right shape, fast enough to matter. That meant solving two problems at once. The first was digital lead flow : routing leads from many sources into Salesforce without asking people to spend their days copying, pasting, and checking records. The second was inbound call volume. As the business grew, Autotorino was handling roughly 100,000 inbound calls a month — more than any team could realistically cover with people alone. Autotorino built the fix in two layers. Riccardo Berta , in CRM and digital, used Zapier to connect lead sources and make Salesforce the system of record. Gabriele Luciani and Michele Spalla , on the innovation team, extended that foundation into voice workflows, pairing Zapier with AI to catch the calls human teams couldn't reach. Riccardo's build returned 2,394 hours to the CRM team Before the build, lead handling was manual. An inquiry might arrive through a brand landing page, a form, a lead ad, or email. Someone then keyed it into Salesforce, matched it to the right process, and moved to the next one. Necessary work, but the kind that drains a team: slow, error-prone, and a poor use of skilled people who should be talking to customers. Riccardo rebuilt that layer as production workflows in Zapier. Instead of forcing very different lead types through one oversized process, the team built separate workflows for separate triggers. Typeform submissions, Facebook Lead Ads , Outlook-based flows, and brand-specific landing pages each got their own path into Salesforce. On the heavier flows, AI enriched or classified the incoming data before the final record was written. Each lead source got the handling it needed, and Salesforce stayed clean on the other side. 109 Salesforce-writing Zaps now run across the business, each built around a specific trigger or process. In 2025, Autotorino calculated the automation returned 2,394 hours to the CRM team and removed a whole class of copy-and-paste errors from the system of record. That kind of data integrity is what makes Salesforce a reliable foundation as teams move toward AI-powered workflows: the models are only as good as the records underneath them. "With the introduction of Zapier, we completely eliminated this workload, allowing our Customer Service team to focus on higher-value activities. Automation also removed the risk of human error, like simple copy/paste mistakes." — Riccardo Berta, CRM & Digital, Autotorino Gabriele's team captured showroom call demand it couldn't afford to miss Digital lead flow was only half the problem. The bigger operational load sat on the phone line. Autotorino was managing around 100,000 inbound calls a month across its dealership network. Those calls came into numbers assigned to individual showrooms, so the problem started at the showroom before it ever became a network-wide one. The business already ran a multi-step handling model across dealerships, a business development center, and external call centers. Even so, it still couldn't answer every call the way it wanted to, and hiring more people into the same process wasn't the answer. That's where the innovation team stepped in. Gabriele and Michele started with a smaller, controlled version of the problem: an early pilot that used Zapier to turn recorded messages into Salesforce leads across a group of dealerships. The pilot now handles roughly 1,500 client requests a month — calls that used to go unanswered. Gabriele estimates the recovered after-sales demand at roughly €150,000 in net profit influenced. From there, the team went further, building a more interactive workflow that combined Zapier with ElevenLabs voice technology. The stack varied by use case, but the pattern held: capture the customer interaction, process it through AI steps, filter and format the output through Zapier, then write the result into Salesforce so the business could act on it. In one production workflow, the architecture ran through AssemblyAI, OpenAI, Zapier, and Salesforce: recorded audio was transcribed, requests were classified against Autotorino's internal framework, and the structured output was routed into the CRM. When the team hit accuracy limits, they refined prompts, split the AI step into smaller parts, and tuned until the workflow produced data the business could trust. "The pilot showed us something simple: calls we thought were lost could actually be captured, structured, and put in front of the sales team automatically. Once that was proven, expanding with Zapier and AI wasn't a bet. It was the obvious next step to protect demand we couldn't afford to keep missing." — Gabriele Luciani, Innovation Project Manager, Autotorino Automation gave Autotorino safer scale and new visibility Plenty of companies use AI. What's telling about Autotorino is how deliberately the team chose where to use Zapier, where to add AI, and where to keep human judgment in the loop. Leadership was enthusiastic and department leaders were pushing for progress, and the team treated that as a reason to build responsibly rather than a license to roll tools out carelessly. That showed up two ways. First, Zapier ran as a controlled orchestration layer inside specific business workflows. The team focused on known operational problems where automation could be measured, so the system scaled without becoming a free-for-all. Salesforce provided the trusted customer intelligence; Zapier kept it clean, connected, and flowing everywhere it needed to go. Together they gave Autotorino the data discipline that prepares their Salesforce environment for what's coming next in agentic AI. Second, the work created visibility the business didn't have before. Once call handling and lead capture moved through structured workflows, Autotorino could see why people were calling, which showrooms were generating missed demand, and where follow-up was getting lost. Under the old manual process, most of that signal disappeared. Under the new one, it became something the business could analyze. The goal was to move people off repetitive intake and toward higher-value work — less manual entry for the CRM team, and automation catching the calls humans couldn't reasonably cover, so employees could focus where judgment matters most. Zapier connects Autotorino's systems, teams, and AI workflows Autotorino didn't treat automation as an isolated tool for one department. It used Zapier to connect customer demand, AI processing, and Salesforce execution into one system. For Riccardo's team, that meant turning fragmented lead sources into clean CRM records. For Gabriele and Michele, it meant giving voice workflows a reliable path into the business. For leadership, it meant pursuing AI use cases without losing operational discipline. Autotorino took processes that were too manual, too error-prone, or too large to handle consistently, and rebuilt them into systems that keep up with the business. What's next Autotorino is now building an outbound-calling workflow designed to follow up with customers after brand communications and help book the next interaction automatically. If the inbound workflow proved Zapier could help Autotorino capture showroom demand more reliably, the outbound project tests whether the same approach can make follow-up proactive instead of reactive.

title: How Hellbender Builds Physical AI Perception on Ambarella’s Edge Platform
summary: A perception model that runs well on a workstation faces a harder test once it goes into a real robot. It suddenly needs to run on a small, power-limited
body_text: A perception model that runs well on a workstation faces a harder test once it goes into a real robot. It suddenly needs to run on a small, power-limited processor, and every wasted watt becomes heat the machine needs to deal with. The processing also has to keep pace with the physical world as it happens. Hellbender builds for that environment, and in a recent joint webinar the Pittsburgh perception and manufacturing company explained how it uses Ambarella’s edge AI platform to get there. Hellbender designs and manufactures perception, edge AI, and robotics components, and it does all of it under one roof in Pittsburgh. Because the company handles every stage, from a product requirements document through proof of concept, validation testing, and full production, it sees the cost of a silicon decision across the whole product lifecycle, well past the benchmark stage. That full-lifecycle view shaped how the company talked about cost in the webinar. Cost is more than the price of the chip Most hardware conversations focus on unit cost, the bill of materials for the silicon and the board around it, but Hellbender argued that two other costs matter just as much. One is integration cost, the engineering time spent getting models compiled, debugged, and running on a given processor. The other, adaptability cost, tends to become an issue later. It is the non-recurring engineering effort and the schedule delay a team faces when a chip cannot support a new model architecture and the design has to be redone in both hardware and software. As the Hellbender team put it, the most expensive chip can be the low-BOM processor that forces a full redo the following year. The architecture question behind physical AI Perception has been shifting from convolutional networks toward transformer-based models, and the effect of that shift goes beyond accuracy. Transformers rely on operations such as dynamic attention, positional encodings, and dynamic tensor indexing, and those operations do not work well with silicon designed only for fixed-function convolution. When the hardware cannot run them natively, teams write workarounds by hand or accept lower accuracy, and the adaptability cost increases as a result. That flexibility is why Hellbender put Ambarella silicon at the center of its perception work. Physical AI leans heavily on the newer operator set, whether the task is dense 3D reconstruction, a vision transformer, an on-device vision language model, or one of the vision-language-action architectures now emerging in robotics. A processor that keeps up as models change lets a robotics team design a board today without stranding it against next year’s model. Efficiency is a whole-system problem Power efficiency is important for reasons that go beyond battery life. Silicon that wastes power produces more heat, and getting rid of that heat means adding thermal mass. The heavier the heatsink, the larger the motors and batteries the machine needs to carry it, which has an effect on payload and reduces flight or run time. In an untethered robot or a drone, an inefficient processor ends up shaping the size and capability of the entire machine, so performance per watt becomes a system-level constraint that engineers must account for. What ran in the demo Running on an Ambarella N1 processor, a high-throughput engine built for large-memory workloads such as LLMs and vision language models, Hellbender showed several perception models working simultaneously in real time, including object detection, depth, optical flow, and an overhead map, together with live vision language model queries run against the scene on the device itself. The perception happened locally, next to the sensor, which is what an edge platform for physical AI is meant to do. Ambarella’s compact CV-series processors cover the lower-power end of the same family, built for computer vision and safety-critical real-time loops. For teams that would rather not start from a blank compiler, Hellbender pointed to Ambarella’s Developer Zone for onboarding. The DevZone provides a library of models already quantized and optimized for specific Ambarella chips, which lets a developer evaluate options and benchmark throughput, power draw, and memory against real targets before committing to a board layout. The Hellbender team also described compiling frontier models directly from PyTorch and ONNX, including recent systems such as DINOv3 and DepthAnything3, and using the platform’s mixed-precision and optimization tooling to hold accuracy while improving efficiency on live systems. Those figures come from Hellbender’s own production work. Watch the webinar One key takeaway from the session is that a processor should be judged on how well it will handle the models a team has not built yet. For its own robotics work, that reasoning led Hellbender to Ambarella’s platform. Check out the webinar here .

title: AI job search tips: 9 AI tools to help you land your next job
summary: These AI resume builders, AI cover letter generators, and other AI job search tools will help streamline the job search and application process.
body_text: From writing your resume for you to automating networking emails, there are tons of ways AI can help streamline your job search . But more importantly, AI can also help you cut through the noise, secure interviews, and impress hiring managers—as long as you use it well. According to a survey from Software Finder , 75% of job seekers use AI tools as part of their job search, with 14% using AI throughout the entire application process. Those who did were more likely to secure a higher-paying job than their previous role (77% compared to 48% of those who didn't use AI). But there are also a lot of bad ways to use AI for job searching, so I scoured the trove of AI job search tools, use cases, and how-tos out there to find the best options. These are the nine tools I'll use next time I'm looking for a job—I hope they help you too. How to use AI to find and land a job There are hundreds of impressive AI-powered job search tools out there. I haven't done in-depth testing on all of them, but the ones I feature below are all well-reviewed and worked as promised in my limited experience with them. If you find that the tool itself isn't quite right for you, don't write off the intention behind the app—keep searching till you find the one that works for you. AI resume builders to help draft and format your resume AI job matching tools to help you find good-fit roles Zapier to automate your job search and applications AI resume optimization tools to tailor your resume for specific roles AI cover letter generators to write a cover letter draft Gemini for Google Sheets to personalize networking at scale AI-powered interview coaching tools for interview practice and feedback AI-powered negotiation tools to get the best offer Your brain for being a human 1. AI resume builders (to help draft and format your resume) Condensing an entire job into three high-impact bullet points is no easy feat, and if you're like most humans, there's nothing you dread more than talking about yourself. I've easily lost hours staring at a blinking cursor, writing, deleting, rewriting, condensing—and on and on. An AI resume writer—like Kickresume , Teal , Huntr , and Resume Worded , among others—will do most of that work for you. All you need to do is fill in your job title. Then the AI resume builder will use AI to come up with relevant bullet points. You can ask the tool to generate as many bullets as you need, then choose those most relevant to your actual work experience. The tools can also write your resume summary, education, skills, and other sections. Once the writing part is handled, you choose from a bunch of design templates and customize colors, fonts, and more to make it feel true to your personal brand. Here's an example of a completed AI-generated resume from Kickresume: Source: Kickresume AI resume tools will pull together a draft that's most of the way there for you to work with. Then all you have to do is edit and add your unique-as-a-snowflake personality. 2. AI job matching tools (to help you find good-fit roles) Sorting through job listings, hunting down requirements and salary ranges, and doing your due diligence on the company culture all eat up valuable energy you could be spending on impressing hiring managers and securing the right role. That's where AI job matching platforms can help: they use AI to match you with job listings likely to be a good fit for both sides, based on your skills, experience, and what you're looking for in a company or position. Platforms like Talentprise , ResumeNerd , Autojob , and Sonara are all good options here. With Talentprise, for example, you'll complete a series of questions on your preferences for a job (like location, willingness to relocate, remote vs. in-office, and when you're available to start) and fill out your "biography," which covers resume stuff like work experience, skills, and education. Then, you'll complete the Talentprise assessment, which measures personality and work traits, along with your values and motivation, to create a holistic profile for you. Then Talentprise's AI matches you with relevant job listings on the site and surfaces your profile to those recruiters. So once you complete your profile, "applying" to best-fit jobs is as close to a passive endeavor as you could hope for. LinkedIn has also added some AI-powered tools for job seekers with a LinkedIn Premium subscription. From the job listing page, paid users will see "Determine your fit and how to stand out" along with a few sample prompts. It's a chatbot-like experience, and you can ask the AI questions like "Am I a good fit?" and "How can I best position myself?" You can also get AI help to tailor your resume for the job and create a cover letter. 3. Zapier (to automate the job search and applications) If you've been job hunting for a while, you've probably found yourself drafting nearly identical email responses to recruiters and hiring managers over and over. It's tedious, but short of using the same email template for every response—not usually a winning strategy—what can you do? With Zapier, you can connect your Gmail inbox with thousands of apps and whatever AI model you prefer, so you can automate bespoke emails . For example, when a recruiter's message lands in your inbox, you can automatically label it as "job hunt." From there, AI can analyze the context of the email, generate a personalized response, and even create a follow-up task in your to-do list app . All you have to do is review the response and hit send. You can also use Zapier to access and take action in all your apps straight from your AI assistant if that's where you spend most of your time. Learn more about how to use Zapier to make your job search less of a full-time job . Try Zapier 4. AI resume optimization tools (to tailor your resume for specific roles) The reality of applying for jobs now is much different from what it was a decade ago. Today, many recruiters and hiring managers rely on algorithms and automated applicant tracking systems (ATS) to scan applicant resumes for the right keywords. If those terms don't feature in your resume, you may get kicked to the "no thanks" pile well before a human ever sets eyes on your application—even if your skills and experience are actually a perfect fit. AI optimization tools, like Teal , Enhancv , Kickresume , Resume Worded , Huntr , and SkillSyncer , ensure your resume makes it past discerning ATS algorithms and into the "interview please" pile. These tools compare your resume, cover letter , and even LinkedIn profile against the keywords found in the job listing you select. They rate how well your resume matches with the role and offer suggestions for how to better optimize your resume for each job. Here's what a match rate report looks like in SkillSyncer. Many of the above tools can analyze and grade your LinkedIn profile, too. Careerflow is another option for that. The tool provides actionable suggestions to optimize your LinkedIn and an interactive AI wizard to help you put those suggestions into action—all in a compact and easy-to-use Chrome extension. 5. AI cover letter generators (to write a cover letter draft) Writing personalized cover letters for each role is possibly the biggest time suck when applying to jobs—but it's also necessary to make an impression. You can use ChatGPT (or any AI chatbot) to write a cover letter . Or you can go with a purpose-built AI-powered cover letter generator like Kickresume and CoverDoc.ai to make the process a whole lot faster and easier. Provide some basic details about the job you're applying for, your preferred writing style, and your LinkedIn profile, and the tool will generate a personalized cover letter draft for you. Here's what CoverDoc came up with based on my own LinkedIn profile and the job listing from the screenshot above. I'd change a thing or two, but it's a solid start! A specialized AI cover letter tool like CoverDoc streamlines the prompt process, but if you're already comfortable using another tool, just about any generative AI writing tool can take care of your cover letter too. I hope it goes without saying that you'll need to review and edit the cover letter to make sure it accurately reflects your skills and experiences and showcases your personality. But starting with a solid draft from an AI tool can be a huge boost in the initial stages of the job application process. 6. Gemini for Google Sheets AI function (to personalize networking at scale) Networking —when done in a tasteful, genuine way—can be an effective way to connect with potential employers and industry contacts. But it can be challenging to personalize these messages at scale. That's why most cold outreach is, well, crap. One approach is to use AI to generate personalized outreach messages en masse. Input a list of recipients and some basic information about each person (e.g., their name, job title, and company). Then you can prompt Gemini to generate a unique message for each person based on this data. The new AI function works much like a typical formula: you type =AI and, within parentheses, your prompt, and specify which cells Gemini should reference. You can keep it simple like this, or ask Gemini to further personalize messaging based on the recipient's LinkedIn profile, tweets, psychological AI, and post engagement. To use the AI function, you'll need a paid Google Workspace account that includes Gemini for Google Sheets. Alternatively, you can use the GPT for Sheets add-on for free. It takes a few more steps to get set up (you can find a detailed how-to from Expandi ), but it will ultimately land you the same functionality. Once again, you'll need to review each message and make sure it's authentic to who you are as a professional, but this tool can streamline the outreach process by a massive amount. 7. AI-powered interview coaching tools (for interview practice and feedback) Interviews can be nerve-racking , but AI-powered interview coaching tools like Interviews by AI , Interviewer.AI , Huru , and AIApply can help you practice and get feedback in a low-stakes environment. You can also use Gemini Live in the same way. These tools simulate a real interview and give you personalized feedback based on your responses. It can help you identify areas where you need to improve, like body language, tone of voice, or specific interview questions you struggled with. Some tools even tailor the questions you're asked based on common job titles or even custom job descriptions you provide. By practicing with these tools, you'll feel more confident and prepared for those higher-stakes real interviews. You'll also have a better sense of what to expect, which can help calm your nerves and let you focus on nailing that first impression. There are even real-time AI tools like Final Round's Interview Copilot to help guide you through active interviews in real-time. 8. AI-powered negotiation tools (to get the best offer) Negotiating your salary can be a fraught process—especially if you're not sure what a fair salary range looks like for your position and experience. AI-powered compensation tools like Payscale can help. These tools use AI to analyze data from thousands of job listings and salary surveys to provide you with an estimate of what you should earn based on details like the job title and your experience, education, and location. They can also offer insight into the benefits and perks you should ask for—like flexible hours or remote work options . Plus, you can fill out granular information on any existing job offers you have to see how they stack up. You can even use an AI chatbot to help judge a job offer , sussing out whether the offer is fair, identifying additional salary or benefits to ask for, and even running through mock negotiations. By using these tools to research salaries before you sit down at the negotiating table, you'll have a better sense of what to expect and be better equipped to make a strong case for what you deserve. 9. Your brain (for being a human) AI can add a ton of speed—and scale—to your job hunt. But quick reminder: both you and the hiring manager are human. When you're applying to and interviewing for a new job, your application materials need to speak to who you are and what you're looking for in a role and company. And they need to be honest: your new company will figure it out very quickly if you don't actually have the skills and strengths the robot made it sound like you have. As more job seekers turn to AI—and hiring managers drown in heavily AI-generated applications—it's more important than ever to humanize and differentiate your job hunt. While AI can help you move more quickly, it's always worth investing the time to ensure the results represent you, the human. Not to mention, other applicants will be using AI, too, so if you don't humanize your application materials, you won't be able to cut through the noise. The most recent update was in August 2026.

title: Communities receive over $700,000 from Alliant Energy & Alliant Energy Foundation
summary: Communities receive over $700,000 from Alliant Energy & Alliant Energy Foundation
body_text: Communities receive over $700,000 from Alliant Energy & Alliant Energy Foundation Grants awarded to194 organizations across Iowa and Wisconsin MADISON, Wis. (August 10, 2026) – In its second Community Grant cycle of the year, Alliant Energy and the Alliant Energy Foundation awarded $708,599 to various causes and nonprofits across Iowa and Wisconsin. All Community Grant recipients seek to make an impact in Alliant Energy’s four focus areas: Community safety and engagement, environmental stewardship, workforce readiness and hunger and housing. Community safety and engagement: Improvements for emergency services and over $130,000 in grants covered 40 communities in first responder organizations including police, fire and EMS departments. This support assisted with the purchase or upgrades of vital equipment. Grants will also support projects and events that foster community connections, including fairs, playground enhancements and other local festivals. Hunger and housing: Organizations that provide household essentials, food assistance through food pantries, meal outreach and delivery programs were awarded over $210,000 in grants in 30 communities. Initiatives providing transition and permanent housing support were also included, helping meet critical needs and support long-term stability in communities. Environmental stewardship: Conservation projects focused on protecting natural habitats, expanding tree and prairie plantings and supporting wildlife received nearly $90,000 in grant funding across 15 communities. Grants will also help advance environmental education initiatives, school programs and support park and trail enhancements that benefit local communities. Workforce readiness: More than $255,000 in grants and scholarships were awarded in this cycle, to support programs that help prepare future generations for success through education, skill development and hands-on learning opportunities. Grants supported programs in 32 communities, including youth agriculture initiatives, school gardens, farm education and innovation, libraries and bookmobiles and STEM programming. The Alliant Energy Foundation is governed by a board of directors consisting of officers of Alliant Energy Corporation or its subsidiaries, which periodically reviews grant program guidelines. The Foundation, which is funded solely by Alliant Energy shareowners, seeks to further the corporation’s goal of being a good corporate citizen and contributing member of society. About Alliant Energy Alliant Energy Corporation (NASDAQ: LNT) provides regulated energy service to more than 1 million electric and 435,000 natural gas customers across Iowa and Wisconsin. Alliant Energy's mission is to deliver energy solutions and exceptional service customers and communities count on – safely, efficiently and responsibly. Interstate Power and Light Company (IPL) and Wisconsin Power and Light Company (WPL) are Alliant Energy's two wholly-owned subsidiaries. For more information, visit alliantenergy.com and follow Alliant Energy on LinkedIn , Facebook , Instagram and X . title: RFI Tracking: Stop Losing Requests in Email and Spreadsheets (August 2026)
summary: Fix the gaps that let RFIs vanish across email and disconnected tools. A practical RFI tracking guide updated for August 2026.
body_text: Your RFI tracking best practices are only as good as the system holding the record. When that record is split between email chains, a shared spreadsheet, and a drawing set in a separate folder, things fall through the gaps, and you end up taking the hit for delays that were never really yours to own. Here's what a tighter process actually looks like. TLDR: Email and spreadsheets break RFI tracking because no tool ties the question to the sheet, the owner, or the deadline. A well-structured RFI has one question, an exact drawing location, a proposed solution, attachments, and a stated schedule impact. Flag any RFI past 75% of its response window, follow up in writing, and log the date so the delay is on record. Projects running above roughly 10 RFIs per $1M in value signal incomplete design, and owners now track that rate as a KPI. Constructable pins RFIs to the exact spot on the drawing, sorts open items by ball-in-court assignment, and you can create an RFI right on the drawings without ever having to leave. Why email and disconnected tools break RFI workflows A question leaves someone's inbox and disappears into a thread. No due date attached, no record of who owns the answer, no way to tell whether the field crew waiting on it ever got word. The trouble sits in the design of the tools, not the people using them. Email was built for correspondence, spreadsheets for tracking rows, shared drives for storage. None of them tie a question to the exact sheet it references, and none carry accountability forward once the message is sent. So a response lands three replies deep in a chain the superintendent was never copied on. A spreadsheet log drifts out of sync the moment two people edit it at once. The drawing that prompted the question lives in a different construction drawing management system entirely. Split across those disconnected tools, email-based RFIs produce predictable failures: questions that vanish into inboxes and duplicate requests that pile up. This is precisely why RFI management in construction breaks down the way it does. RFIs as a risk management and accountability system An RFI is a paper trail before it is anything else. Every question logged, every response documented, every date stamped becomes the record you fall back on when a delay dispute lands on your desk months later. When RFIs live in email and disconnected tools, that record fractures. For a deeper look at RFI management in construction , treating RFI tracking as accountability infrastructure changes what you protect: Ball-in-court clarity, so responsibility for a stalled question is never ambiguous and delays trace back to the party actually holding it. Timestamped response history, giving you defensible dates when an owner or architect questions why the schedule slipped. Cost and schedule impact tied to each question, so the financial weight of a slow answer is visible while there is still time to act. Lose that trail and you take the hit for delays you never had a chance to prevent. What every well-structured RFI needs An RFI that gets answered in one pass keeps the job moving. A vague one bounces back with a follow-up question, and every round trip adds days to a cycle you were trying to shorten. The difference comes down to what you put in the request before you hit send. Choosing the right RFI management software for GCs starts with knowing what a well-structured RFI carries. Five things: One question, and only one. Bundling three unrelated issues into a single submission means the whole thing stalls until the slowest answer comes back. Industry guidance is consistent on sticking to one question per RFI . The exact location. Sheet number, detail callout, revision, and area, so the designer opens the right drawing instead of hunting for the spot you meant. A proposed solution wherever you have one. Giving the reviewer something to approve or reject beats asking them to author an answer from scratch. Supporting attachments. A marked-up sheet or a site photo shows the condition faster than a paragraph describing it. A stated schedule impact tied to a real deadline. When the reviewer sees which crew is waiting and when, the needed-by date carries weight. Leave any of these out and you hand the designer a reason to write back with a question of their own. Submission timing and workflow sequencing Timing is where most RFI slippage starts. Teams relying on inadequate drawing management software compound the problem: a question raised too late lands in someone's inbox when the ball-in-court party is already buried, so the answer waits, and the field waits with it. Good sequencing keeps that from happening. A few habits keep RFIs moving in the right order: Raise the question at the point of discovery, not at the end of the day when the detail is half-remembered and the drawing reference is fuzzy. Route it to the right ball-in-court party first, so it does not bounce between the architect, engineer, and owner before anyone owns the answer. Tie the RFI to the schedule activity it affects, so the due date reflects when the field actually needs the answer, not an arbitrary two-week default. Batch related questions where it makes sense, so reviewers see the full context instead of piecemeal follow-ups. Sequenced this way, the question reaches the right person while there is still room to respond before the work is blocked. Ball-in-court tracking and escalation protocols One owner per stage keeps an RFI from stalling in the quiet space between people. The right construction communication and collaboration tools make this handoff visible. When the GC submits, the ball sits with the architect. When the answer comes back, it moves to the PM to distribute. Name that person every time the RFI changes hands. Build the escalation on dates, not memory: Flag any RFI that has passed 75 percent of its response window. Send a written follow-up, never a verbal one, and log the date it went out. Note the potential schedule impact on that follow-up so the delay is on record. A response that lands without answering the question is not a closed RFI. Reopen it, re-route it to the party who still owes the answer, and keep the original thread intact so the follow-up reads as one continuous record instead of a fresh request. Common RFI mistakes that cost time and margin A handful of habits show up on almost every job, and each one quietly extends a cycle you were trying to close. Bundling several questions into one RFI, which stalls the whole thing behind the slowest answer. Proceeding on a verbal direction nobody wrote down, so the record splits the moment a dispute starts. Letting a request sit past its window with no follow-up. Writing an RFI for something the contract documents already answer. Sending a needed-by date with no stated schedule impact behind it. None of these is carelessness. They are what an unstructured process produces on its own. And the cost compounds fast: across 1,362 projects studied , RFIs averaged 796 per project at roughly $1,080 each, or about $859,680 per project in direct processing alone. Trim a day off each cycle and shave a few dollars off each handoff, and that number moves in your favor. RFI metrics that reveal process health A structured log turns individual questions into a read on how the job is actually running. Watch a handful of numbers, and the workflow problems underneath them show up before they cost you. Metric What it signals Average response time by RFI type Which categories consistently stall and where to push Percentage unanswered within the contractual window Whether ball-in-court parties are meeting their obligations RFI volume per $1M of project value Design completeness and coordination quality Percentage tied to a specific drawing location How traceable your record is when a dispute starts Rate of RFIs that turn into construction change orders How much design ambiguity is converting into cost Volume is the one owners now read most closely. A project running far above the roughly 10-per-$1M benchmark points to incomplete design, poor coordination, or ambiguous specs, and more owners treat that rate as a designer-performance KPI. Pull these into the weekly OAC meeting . (Constructable's Smart Section in meeting minutes makes this super easy.) When response times drift past the contractual window or volume climbs well over the benchmark, escalate to the design team or owner in writing while there is still schedule left to protect. None of it works if the log lives in scattered inboxes, so the numbers depend on one centralized record. How Constructable keeps RFIs from getting lost Every breakdown this post has walked through traces back to the same root: tools that were never built to hold a question in one place. Constructable closes those gaps through how the system is built, not through features bolted on after the fact. RFIs pin to the exact spot on the sheet they reference, with markups, responses, and comments all tied to that pin. The context lives on the drawing instead of in a separate log you cross-reference by hand, which is the pattern that defines drawing-centric collaboration workflows . An RFI stays in draft, private and silent, until you deliberately open it, so no one gets a premature notification and the record stays clean. Open RFIs sort by ball-in-court assignment, pushing the most pressing action items to the top without any manual filtering. When you close and distribute, AI drafts the distribution message from the response itself, taking the friction out of the final step email workflows tend to skip. The AI Answer Engine links every answer back to its primary source, so a response points to the drawing, document, or log entry behind it. Subcontractors can open draft RFIs directly, with a default manager auto-assigned, clearing the bottleneck of routing every field question through a GC first. It's the same pin-to-plan logic that drives plan-linked punch lists and issue management . If you want to see how it holds up on a real project, book a demo and put your own RFI log in front of it. Final thoughts on running a tighter RFI workflow None of the habits covered here require a total overhaul, just a consistent structure applied at the right points in the cycle. One question per request, a stated schedule impact, a named ball-in-court owner, and a log that lives in one place, that is the whole system. Get those pieces right and your response times shrink, your disputes get shorter, and your field crew spends less time waiting. Talk to us if you want to see what that looks like in practice with Constructable . FAQs What's the difference between managing RFIs in Constructable vs. email and spreadsheets? Email and spreadsheets break RFI accountability the moment a response lands in a thread the superintendent wasn't copied on, or two people edit the log at once. Constructable , as a connected system, pins each RFI to the exact sheet location it references, with responses, markups, and ball-in-court assignments all tied to that pin, so the record stays in one place instead of fracturing across inboxes and disconnected files. How do I write an RFI that gets answered in one pass? Include one question only, the exact sheet and detail callout, a proposed solution where you have one, supporting attachments like a marked-up sheet or site photo, and a stated schedule impact tied to a real deadline. Each of those elements removes a reason for the reviewer to write back with a follow-up question before answering yours. What RFI metrics should I be tracking to catch workflow problems early? Track average response time by RFI type, the percentage of RFIs unanswered within the contractual window, volume per $1M of project value, the percentage tied to a specific drawing location, and the rate of RFIs that convert into change orders. Volume is the number owners now watch most closely: a project running well above roughly 10 RFIs per $1M points to incomplete design or ambiguous specs, and pulling these numbers into the weekly OAC meeting gives you time to escalate in writing while schedule room still exists. Should I be tracking RFI ball-in-court manually or through a dedicated system? A dedicated system with named ball-in-court assignments at every handoff beats manual tracking. When you rely on memory or a spreadsheet, the accountability gap between submission and response has no owner, follow-ups go unlogged, and you lose the written record you need when a delay dispute starts. Constructable sorts open RFIs by ball-in-court assignment automatically, so the most pressing items stay visible without manual filtering. Can subcontractors submit RFIs directly in Constructable without going through the GC? Yes. Subcontractors can create limited draft RFIs directly within Constructable , with a default manager auto-assigned and notified on draft creation. title: Partner Relationship Management Software for ISVs
summary: What PRM software does, when ISVs actually need it, and why marketplace sellers need PRM that resolves deals against AWS, Azure and GCP.
body_text: Partner relationship management (PRM) software is a system for running a partner program — onboarding, tiers, commissions, deal registration and co-sell tracking — in one place. Independent software vendors (ISVs) that sell through cloud marketplaces need marketplace-native PRM, where partner activity resolves against real AWS, Azure and Google Cloud transactions. One of the most common questions a new VP of Partnerships asks is deceptively simple: where does our partner program actually live? For most ISVs the honest answer is a spreadsheet, a shared inbox, and three people’s memories — and every quarter that passes, more partner revenue leaks through the gaps between them. The cost isn’t abstract. Registrations go unanswered, commissions get disputed, and partners quietly stop bringing you deals because working with you is harder than working with someone else. Here’s how to decide what to do about it. What is partner relationship management software? Partner relationship management (PRM) software is a platform for managing the companies that sell your product for you — resellers, referral partners, and co-sell partners. It gives partners a portal to register deals, track commissions and complete training, and gives you one system of record for everything those partners do. A customer relationship management (CRM) system manages your relationship with buyers. PRM manages your relationship with the partners who bring you buyers. The two overlap in the pipeline they describe, but they answer different questions: the CRM asks “where is this deal?”, the PRM asks “who sourced this deal, what do they earn, and what do they need from us to close it?” Most ISVs meet PRM the same way. First a partner program starts in a spreadsheet. Then the spreadsheet starts losing registrations. Then someone gets asked to evaluate PRM tooling — usually right after a commission dispute. What does PRM software actually do? A partner relationship management (PRM) platform earns its place by taking over five jobs that otherwise live in spreadsheets and email: Partner onboarding and journeys : Structured paths that take a partner from signed agreement to first registered deal, with training and certifications along the way. Partner tiers : Levels like Registered → Silver → Gold → Platinum that recognize partner commitment and unlock benefits — a topic deep enough that we cover tier and commission design in its own guide: channel partner relationship management, explained . Commission plans : The rules that determine what each partner earns — referral fees, reseller margins, co-sell revenue splits — and when the payment triggers. Deal registration : The mechanism by which a partner formally claims an opportunity, so the deal is protected from channel conflict. We walk through the full lifecycle in our guide to deal registration software . Collaboration and visibility : Shared views of pipeline, files, and next steps, so neither side runs the partnership over email threads. Each job is simple on its own. The compounding value is that one partner record connects all five. When do you actually need PRM software? You need PRM software when the volume of partner activity exceeds what a spreadsheet and a responsive partner manager can track — typically somewhere past ten active partners or a handful of registrations a month. Below that, tooling adds process without adding revenue. Above it, the spreadsheet starts costing you deals. The honest way to decide is to score yourself on two axes: how complex your partner program is, and how much of your revenue transacts through cloud marketplaces. Low marketplace volume High marketplace volume Simple program (few partners, one commission model) A spreadsheet is fine. Revisit in two quarters. You need marketplace operations tooling first — PRM can wait until the program itself grows. Complex program (tiers, multiple commission models, 10+ active partners) Generic PRM works. Marketplace-native PRM buys you nothing extra here. Marketplace-native PRM — this is the quadrant where generic tools break, because partner economics and marketplace transactions have to reconcile. Two of those four quadrants don’t need PRM software at all. If you’re in one of them, a simpler answer will serve you better — and you should take it. Why do marketplace sellers outgrow generic PRM? Generic PRM tools assume the deal closes wherever your CRM says it closes. For ISVs selling through AWS Marketplace, Azure Marketplace and Google Cloud Marketplace, the deal actually closes as a marketplace transaction — a private offer accepted by the buyer, often routed through a reseller as a Channel Partner Private Offer (CPPO). That one difference breaks three things in a generic tool. Deal registration can’t confirm the registered deal ever transacted. Commission plans can’t calculate margin on a transaction the PRM never sees. Partner tiers can’t count marketplace revenue toward tier criteria, because the revenue lives in a marketplace management portal the PRM doesn’t read. Marketplace-native PRM closes that loop: the partner registers the deal, the deal resolves to the marketplace transaction, and the commission calculates from what actually transacted. The registration is the claim. The transaction is the proof. The commission is the settlement between them. If your partner motion runs through the hyperscalers, this is the requirement to put at the top of the evaluation — ahead of portal branding, ahead of training modules, ahead of everything demoware is good at. For the co-sell side of that motion, Partnerships 101 covers how alliance teams build it. How to evaluate PRM software as an ISV The evaluation criteria that separate PRM platforms for a marketplace-first ISV, in the order they should be weighted: Marketplace transaction resolution : Can a registered deal be tied to the AWS, Azure or Google Cloud transaction that fulfills it? This is the criterion generic PRM fails. Commission model coverage : Referral fees, reseller margins, co-sell revenue splits and finder’s fees are different payment structures. A program usually needs more than one. CRM integration depth : Registrations should pre-fill from Salesforce or HubSpot opportunities, and acceptance should write back — otherwise you’ve bought a second data-entry surface. Partner experience : A portal partners actually log into, with their tier, their commissions, and their open registrations visible without asking you. Time to first value : A partner program that takes two quarters to configure loses momentum before it starts. Ask every vendor what week one looks like. A vendor that scores well on all five is rare. A vendor that can’t answer the first one isn’t built for the way you sell. How Suger helps with partner relationship management Platforms like Suger build PRM directly on top of marketplace infrastructure, which is the architectural difference the previous sections describe. Suger PRM includes a partner console and portal , partner tiers with up to six configurable levels, commission plans covering all four commission types with standard defaults and per-partner custom plans, and deal registration that links each registered deal to a CRM opportunity and a co-sell record. Because the same platform manages marketplace listings, private offers and co-sell across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and other marketplaces, partner activity and marketplace transactions live in one system — the loop generic PRM leaves open. Frequently asked questions What is partner relationship management software? Partner relationship management (PRM) software is a platform for managing reseller, referral and co-sell partners. It typically includes a partner portal, deal registration, partner tiers, commission plans, and training — one system of record for everything your partners do with you. What is the difference between PRM and CRM? A CRM manages your relationship with customers; a PRM manages your relationship with the partners who sell to customers on your behalf. PRM adds partner-specific structures a CRM lacks: deal registration, commission plans, partner tiers and a partner-facing portal. When should an ISV buy PRM software? When partner activity outgrows a spreadsheet — usually past ten active partners or several deal registrations a month, or the first time a commission is disputed. Before that point, lightweight tracking is fine; after it, lost registrations start costing real revenue. What is marketplace-native PRM? Marketplace-native PRM is partner relationship management software that resolves partner activity against cloud marketplace transactions. A registered deal links to the AWS, Azure or Google Cloud transaction that fulfills it, so commissions and tier credit calculate from revenue that actually transacted. Do I need PRM software if I only sell through cloud marketplaces directly? No. If you have no resellers, referral partners or co-sell partners, you need marketplace operations tooling, not PRM. PRM becomes relevant the day another company starts sourcing or influencing your deals. How is PRM different from a partner portal? A partner portal is the partner-facing surface of a PRM — where partners log in, register deals and check commissions. The PRM is the full system behind it: the tier definitions, commission rules, registration workflow and reporting the portal exposes. Takeaways Score your program on two axes — program complexity and marketplace volume — before evaluating anything. Two of the four quadrants don’t need PRM at all. If your deals close as marketplace transactions, make transaction resolution your first evaluation criterion. It’s the one generic PRM tools fail. Buy PRM when the spreadsheet starts losing registrations, not when the partner count hits a round number. Weight time-to-first-value heavily. A partner program stalls faster than a PRM implementation finishes. Suger’s PRM runs partner tiers, commissions and deal registration on the same platform that executes your marketplace transactions. See how it fits your program on the Suger PRM page , or start with the PRM documentation .
